ety: From Middle English gendre, borrowed from Old French gendre, borrowed from Latin genere (“type, kind”). Doublet of genre and genus. The verb developed after the noun. Displaced native Old English hād (“sex, gender”).

s.def: A narrow ornamental fabric or braid of silk, wool, or cotton, often stiffened with metallic wire or coarse cord running through it, used as trimming for dresses, curtains, furniture, etc. Also guimpe.

s.def: A small round particle of substance; a drop.
ex: A civilized hotel is a little urban globule floating like scum on a rustic pool.

ety: Etymology tree Latin globus Proto-Indo-European *-lós Proto-Indo-European *-elós Proto-Italic *-elos Latin -ulus Latin globuluslbor. French globulebor. English globule Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Indo-European *-iHnos Proto-Italic *-īnos Latin -īnusder. Old French -inbor. Middle English -in English -ineclip. English -in English globulin From globule + -in.

s.def: Any of a group of simple proteins, soluble in water only in the presence of salts, that are coagulated by heat

ety: From German Glockenspiel (literally “bells-set”).

s.def: A musical instrument of the percussion idiophone family of instruments. Like the xylophone, it has tuned bars arranged like the keys on a piano. It is smaller in size and higher in pitch than the xylophone, and the bars are made of metal instead of wood.

ety: Borrowed from Latin glomerātus, perfect passive participle of glomero (“to glomerate”), see -ate (verb-forming suffix) and -ate (adjective-forming suffix).

s.def: To gather or curl into a ball; to collect (threads, etc.) into a spherical form or mass.
ex: glomerated fig tree

s.def: Gathered together in a somewhat spherical mass or dense cluster; conglomerate.
ex: glomerate gland
glomerate flower
glomerate mass of crystals

ety: Diminutive of Latin glomus ball.

s.def: A head or dense cluster of flowers, formed by condensation of a cyme, as in the flowering dogwood.
ex: glomerules of the thallus
O. fragrantissima[…]Inflorescence of alternate sessile glomerules ½–¾ in. diam., each containing 8–12 nearly sessile heads[…]

s.def: A glomerulus.
ex: The function of the glomerule is to separate the superfluous water from the blood

s.def: A globule of metal.

ety: From Middle English *gloom, *glom, from Old English glōm (“gloaming, twilight, darkness”), from Proto-West Germanic *glōm, from Proto-Germanic *glōmaz (“gleam, shimmer, sheen”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰley- (“to gleam, shimmer, glow”). The English word is cognate with Norwegian glom (“transparent membrane”), Scots gloam (“twilight; faint light; dull gleam”).

s.def: Darkness, dimness, or obscurity.
ex: the gloom of a forest, or of midnight

s.def: A depressing, despondent, or melancholic atmosphere.
ex: Although it's always crowded You still can find some room For broken-hearted lovers To cry there in their gloom.

s.def: Cloudiness or heaviness of mind; melancholy; aspect of sorrow; low spirits; dullness.
ex: A sullen gloom and furious disorder prevailed by fits.

s.def: A drying oven used in gunpowder manufacture.
To be dark or gloomy.
ex: Around all the dark forest gloomed.

s.def: To look or feel sad, sullen or despondent.
ex: Ciss was a big, dark-complexioned, pug-faced young woman who seemed to be glooming about something.
"Is Maggie then astonishing too?"—and he gloomed out of his window.
He gloomed for some moments above the round-topped table[.]

s.def: To render gloomy or dark; to obscure; to darken.
ex: A black yew gloom'd the stagnant air.

s.def: To fill with gloom; to make sad, dismal, or sullen.
To shine or appear obscurely or imperfectly; to glimmer.

ety: From gloom + -y. Cognate with Saterland Frisian glumig (“dark, gloomy”).

s.def: Not very illuminated; dim because of darkness, especially when appearing depressing or frightening.
ex: The cavern was gloomy.

s.def: Suffering from gloom; melancholy; dejected.
ex: a gloomy temper or countenance

s.def: Someone or something that is gloomy or pessimistic.

ety: From Middle English glorificacion, glorificacioun, from Middle French glorification and its etymon Latin glōrificātiō. By surface analysis, glorify + -ication.

s.def: The act of glorifying or the state of being glorified.
Specifically, the ascension (of Christ or humans) to the glory of heaven.
ex: Christ was guiding evolution toward a state of glorification so that humanity could finally merge with God in eternal perfection.

s.def: The worshiping of a deity; extolment or laudation.
The portrayal of something as being ideal; idealization.

ety: From Middle English glorifien, from Anglo-Norman and Old French glorifier, from Late Latin glōrificō, from Latin glōria + -ficō (“to make”). By surface analysis, glory + -fy. Displaced native Middle English wuldrien (“to glorify”), from Old English wuldrian as well as Middle English stellifien (“to glorify, make stellar”), from Old French stellifier (Medieval Latin stellificāre); see stellify.

s.def: To exalt, or give glory or praise to (something or someone).
To make (something) appear to be more glorious than it is; regard something or someone as excellent baselessly.
ex: Some movies glorify mobsters by making them seem like the cool kids around the block.
Historical dictators are glorified in some countries that are dictatorships and by some political radicals.

s.def: To worship or extol.

ety: From Middle English glorious, from Anglo-Norman glorius and Old French glorïos, from Latin glōriōsus. Displaced native Middle English wulderful, from Old English wuldorfull (“glorious”), among other terms. Equivalent to glory + -ous.

s.def: Exhibiting attributes, qualities, or acts that are worthy of or receive glory.
ex: glorious deeds

s.def: Excellent, wonderful; delightful.
Bright or shining;
Eager for glory or distinction
Excessively proud or boastful.
Ecstatic; hilarious; elated with drink.

ety: From Middle English glory, glorie, from Old French glorie (“glory”), from Latin glōria (“glory, fame, renown, praise, ambition, boasting”). Doublet of gloria. Displaced native Old English wuldor.

s.def: Great beauty and splendor.
Honour, admiration, or distinction, accorded by common consent to a person or thing; high reputation; renown.
That quality in a person or thing which secures general praise or honour.
ex: Deeme it no gloire to swell in tyrannie.
As jewels lose their glory if neglected, So princes their renowns if not respected.

s.def: Worship or praise.
ex: Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men.

s.def: An optical phenomenon, consisting of concentric rings and somewhat similar to a rainbow, caused by sunlight or moonlight interacting with the water droplets that compose mist or clouds, centered on the antisolar or antilunar point.
Victory; success.
ex: But, with United fans in celebratory mood as it appeared their team might snatch glory, they faced an anxious wait as City equalised in stoppage time.

s.def: An emanation of light supposed to shine from beings that are specially holy. It is represented in art by rays of gold, or the like, proceeding from the head or body, or by a disk, or a mere line.
ex: Seen across the dim candle with his moistened eyes, she looked as if she had a glory shining round her head.

s.def: The manifestation of the presence of God as perceived by humans in Abrahamic religions.
Pride; boastfulness; arrogance.
Something glorious.

ety: Probably from a North Germanic language, compare Icelandic glossi (“spark, flame”), glossa (“to flame”); or perhaps from dialectal Dutch gloos (“a glow, flare”), related to West Frisian gloeze (“a glow”), Middle Low German glȫsen (“to smoulder, glow”), German glosen (“to smoulder”); ultimately from Proto-Germanic *glus- (“to glow, shine”), from Proto-Indo-European *ǵʰel- (“to flourish; be green or yellow”). More at glow.

s.def: A surface shine or luster.
A superficially or deceptively attractive appearance.
ex: To me more dear, congenial to my heart, / One native charm than all the gloss of art.

s.def: A brief explanatory note or translation of a foreign, archaic, technical, difficult, complex, or uncommon expression, inserted after the original, in the margin of a document, or between lines of a text.
ex: All this, without a gloss or comment, / He would unriddle in a moment.
He was a prolific annotator - writing around fifty thousand glosses in as many as twenty manuscripts.

s.def: To give a gloss or sheen to.
To make (something) attractive by deception
ex: You have the art to gloss the foulest cause.

s.def: To become shiny.
Used in a phrasal verb: gloss over (“to cover up a mistake or crime, to treat something with less care than it deserves”).
Synonym of glossary, a collection of such notes.
An expression requiring such explanatory treatment.
An extensive commentary on some text.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Hellenic *glṓt͏̌t͏̌ā Ancient Greek γλῶσσᾰ (glôssă) English -al English glossal From Ancient Greek γλῶσσᾰ (glôssă, “a tongue”) + English -al.

s.def: Of or relating to the tongue.

ety: From Middle English glosarie, from Latin glossārium, from Ancient Greek γλῶσσα (glôssa, “tongue”). Doublet of glossarium.

s.def: A list of difficult words or specialized terms used in a particular book or document, or in a particular domain of knowledge, with their definitions; a list of glosses (explanatory annotations).
ex: At the back of the book you can find the glossary.

ety: From gloss- + -ectomy.

s.def: The surgical removal of all or part of the tongue.

ety: From glosso- + -itis.

s.def: An inflammatory condition of the tongue.

ety: From glosso- + -lalia, from Ancient Greek γλῶσσᾰ (glôssă, “tongue; language”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *glōgʰs) + λᾰλῐᾱ́ (lălĭā́, “talking; form of speech, dialect”) (from λᾰ́λος (lắlos, “talkative”) + -ῐ́ᾱ (-ĭ́ā, suffix forming feminine abstract nouns)).

s.def: Speaking a language one does not know, or speaking elaborate but apparently meaningless speech, while in a trance-like state (or, supposedly, under the influence of a deity or spirits); speaking in tongues.
ex: Everything was a labyrinthine amalgam of languages, a towering Babel of puns and glossolalia.

s.def: Synonym of xenoglossy (“knowledge of a language one has never learned”).

ety: Etymology tree English gloss Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Germanic *-gaz Proto-West Germanic *-g Old English -iġ Middle English -y English -y English glossy From gloss + -y.

s.def: Having a smooth, silklike, reflective (shiny) surface.
ex: glossy magazine

s.def: Attention-grabbing and superficially attractive.
ex: The trendy rehabs being pimped by the addiction industry's glossy PR.

s.def: A glossy magazine.
ex: The supermarket glossies are full of celebrity gossip and fad diets.

s.def: A glossy photograph.
A film depicting people with glamorous lifestyles.
Plegadis falcinellus, a medium-sized wading bird with a long, decurved bill.

ety: See gloss.

s.def: Lead glazing used for pottery.
ex: If no decoration is applied, biscuit or glost firing is the final operation in manufacture.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek γλωττῐ́ς (glōttĭ́s)bor. New Latin glōttisbor. English glottis Proto-Indo-European *h₂el- Proto-Indo-European *-is Proto-Indo-European *h₂élisder.? Proto-Italic *-ālis Latin -ālisbor. Old French -albor. ▲ Latin -ālis Old French -elbor. ▲ Latin -ālisbor. Middle English -al English -al English glottal From glottis + -al.

s.def: Of or relating to the glottis.
Articulated with the glottis.
ex: Her Malay was the Malay of the Staate of Lanchap [...] and she spoke it fierily, with crisp glottal checks, with much bubbling reduplication.

s.def: A sound made with the glottis
A plosive sound articulated with the glottis.
The glottal stop symbol, ʔ.
hiatus

ety: Late 16th century borrowing from New Latin glōttis, from Ancient Greek γλωττῐ́ς (glōttĭ́s, “mouth of the windpipe”), from γλῶττᾰ (glôttă, “tongue”) + -ῐς (-ĭs, feminine noun suffix). Cognates include Latin gula.

s.def: The opening between the true vocal cords which is located in the larynx and affects voice modulation through expansion or contraction.

ety: From Middle English glove, glofe, from Old English glōf, *glōfe, *glōfa, ("glove"; weak forms attested only in plural form glōfan (“gloves”)), from Proto-Germanic *galōfô (“glove”), from Proto-Germanic *ga- (“collective and associative prefix”) + Proto-Germanic *lōfô (“flat of the hand, palm”), from Proto-Indo-European *lāp-, *lēp-, *lep- (“flat”). Cognate with Scots gluve, gluive (“glove”), Icelandic glófi (“glove”). Related to Middle English lofe, lufe (“palm of the hand”). More at loof.

s.def: An item of clothing, covering all or part of the hand and fingers, but usually allowing independent movement of the fingers.
ex: I wore gloves to keep my hands warm.
The boxing champ laced on his gloves before the big bout.

s.def: A baseball mitt.
The ability to catch a hit ball.
ex: Frederico had a great glove, but he couldn't hit a curveball, so he never broke into the pros.

s.def: A condom.
A challenge from one to another.
ex: to throw down the glove, i.e. to offer a challenge; to take up the glove, to accept it

s.def: To catch the ball in a baseball mitt.
ex: He gloved the line drive for the third out.

s.def: To put a glove or gloves on.
ex: Maxwell gloved his hand so that he wouldn't leave fingerprints, then pulled the trigger.
After the maids had hatted and gloved the girls, the carriage was summoned and I was carted around one church after another.

s.def: To touch (a delivery) with one's glove while the gloved hand is on the bat. Under the rules of cricket, the batsman is deemed to have hit the ball.
A compartment recessed in an automobile’s dashboard, that usually has a door and can be locked, intended to hold gloves, papers, etc.

ety: The verb is derived from Middle English glouen, glowen (“to give off heat and light without flame; of a thing: to be heated until red hot; to be brightly coloured; to shine brightly; (figurative) to be filled with emotion; of the face, etc.: to turn red, flush; etc.”), and then either: * from Old English glōwan (“to glow”) (a strong verb), from Proto-West Germanic *glōan (“to glow”); or * because the Middle English and modern English words are weak verbs, possibly from Old Norse *glówa, thought…

s.def: To emit heat and light without a flame.
ex: Iron glows red hot when heated to near its melting point.

s.def: Of a fire: to emit heat and light.
ex: The fire was still glowing after ten hours.

s.def: To emit light brightly and steadily as if heated to a high temperature; to shine.
ex: [N]ovv glovv'd the Firmament / VVith living Saphirs: […]

s.def: To be very hot; also, to be on fire; to burn.
Of a colour: to be bright; also, of a thing: to have a bright colour.
ex: The new baby’s room glows with bright, loving colours.
The hills glowed like purple amethysts, the sky glowed topaz and vermilion colours.
[H]is tunic glowed in the richest hues of the Tyrian dye, and the fibulæ, or buckles, by which it was fastened sparkled with emeralds: […]

s.def: Of a person: to display intense emotion.
ex: a healthy glow
The zealots glowed with religious fervor.
You are glowing from happiness!

s.def: Of a person's body or a part of it: to feel hot and often to flush (“become suffused with a reddish colour”) as well, due to an emotional response, exertion, etc.
ex: After their workout, the gymnasts’ faces were glowing.
[H]er cheek glowed while she spoke; but an arch, provokiong smile was on her lips.
"And how do you know that, my sweet Madam?" said the adventurer, turning first deadly pale, and then glowing red.

s.def: To be involved in an (chiefly online) undercover sting operation, especially by American federal agencies.
ex: If this post glows any brighter I'm going to need sunglasses. 😄🕶👌

s.def: To create a threatening online post that may involve violence, and look suspicious enough to attract a police investigation.
To emit (flame).

ety: From an alteration (possibly Scots) of glore, from Middle English glōren, glouren (“to gleam; to glare, glower”); or from glow (“to stare”) (obsolete), and ultimately from a Scandinavian (North Germanic) language. Cognate with Low German gloren (“to flicker; to glimmer”), Dutch gloren, Icelandic glóra. By surface analysis, glow + -er (fossilized frequentative suffix). See more at glare.

s.def: To look or stare with anger.
ex: Now look at this board that I just flung into the dark aisle out o' the way, while Monkbarns was glowering ower a' the silver yonder.
She glowered at me; nothing would quiet her.
[Charles Francis] Harding was a kindly, quiet man, though he seemed to glower through his pince nez spectacles.

s.def: An angry glare or stare.
ex: She sure has an awful glower on her face.

s.def: That which glows or emits light.

ety: From Middle English glouworm; equivalent to glow + worm. Compare cognate German Glühwurm; compare also firefly, lightning bug, and lanternfly.

s.def: The larva or wingless grub-like female of a beetle from the families Phengodidae or Lampyridae that gives out a green light from its abdomen.
ex: The glowworm shows the matin to be near And ’gins to pale his uneffectual fire. Adieu, adieu, adieu! Remember me.
Glories (like glowe-wormes) a farre off, shine bright, But look’d to neere, haue neither heate, nor light.
Ye Glo-worms, whose officious Flame To wandring Mowers shows the way, That in the Night have lost their aim, And after foolish Fires do stray;

s.def: A carnivorous gnat larva in the keroplatid genus Arachnocampa that spins threads to capture insects attracted by its glow.

ety: From Middle English glosen, from Old French gloser, from Medieval Latin glossa. Doublet of gloss and glossa.

s.def: A comment in the margin; explanatory note; gloss; commentary.
ex: The relation of certain words in the original to the practice of my translation may require gloze.

s.def: Flattery.
ex: […] if Virtue aught may crave, or Heav’n, Beware, alike, of factious leagues, impure, And courtly glozes vile.
No tender word or dainty gloze Could give him pleasure half so fine As that which tingled to her blows.

s.def: appearance.
A specious show, a deceit.
ex: Now to plain-dealing; lay these glozes by: Shall we resolve to woo these girls of France?

s.def: To extenuate, explain away, gloss over.
To use flattering language.
ex: So gloz’d the Tempter, and his Proem tun’d; Into the Heart of Eve his words made way,

s.def: To smooth over; to palliate by specious explanation.
To give a shine to (something or someone).

ety: From gluco- + Ancient Greek ἄγων (ágōn), present participle of ἄγω (ágō, “push forward, put in motion; stir up; excite, urge”).

s.def: A peptide hormone, produced by the pancreas, that opposes the action of insulin by stimulating the production of sugar

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek γλεῦκος (gleûkos)der. French glucose English glucose From French, from Ancient Greek γλεῦκος (gleûkos, “wine, must”). By surface analysis, gluco- + -ose; note that -ose is derived from the word glucose.

s.def: A simple monosaccharide (sugar) with a molecular formula of C₆H₁₂O₆; a principle source of energy for cellular metabolism.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *gleyH- Proto-Indo-European *glóh₁ytn̥ Proto-Italic *gloiten Latin glūten Late Latin glūs Old French glubor. Middle English glew English glue From Middle English glew, glue, from Old French glu (“glue, birdlime”), from Late Latin glūs (stem glūt-), from Latin glūten. Related to clay. Partially displaced native Old English līm (“glue”) and ġelīman (“to glue”) (whence modern lime).

s.def: A hard gelatin made by boiling bones and hides, used in solution as an adhesive; or any sticky adhesive substance.
ex: Near-synonyms: adhesive, cement

s.def: Anything that binds two things or people together.
ex: What is a kiss ? Why this, as some approve, / The sure sweet cement, glue, and lime of love.

s.def: A viscid secretion on the surface of certain plants.
join with glue
To join or attach something using glue.
ex: I need to glue the chair-leg back into place.

s.def: To cause something to adhere closely to; to cause to follow attentively.
ex: His eyes were glued to the screen.
Keep your eyes glued to that set until the station signs off. I can assure you that what you will observe is a vast wasteland.

s.def: To apply glue.

ety: From glue + boil + -er.

s.def: A specialized profession practised in the developed world up to the early twentieth century that made, from particularly cattle bones, the adhesives used in for instance paperwork, bookbinding, joinery, ivory inlay.

ety: Probably from Middle Low German glum (“glum”), related to German dialectal glumm (“gloomy, troubled, turbid”). More at gloomy.

s.def: Despondent; moody; sullen.
ex: I[…]frighten people by my glum face.
[…] and the prospect of three more days of teaching before the weekend break, Mr. MacPherson felt unusually glum.
A glummer look replaced the already glum look on Arthur Dent's face.

s.def: To look sullen; to be of a sour countenance; to be glum.
sullenness
ex: That they be deaf and dumb, And play silence and glum

ety: Compare French glumancé. See glume and -aceous.

s.def: Having or consisting of glumes.
ex: glumaceous bracts
glumaceous perianth
glumaceous valves

ety: From Latin gluma (“husk of grain”). The root can also be seen in glubere (“to peel”).

s.def: A basal, membranous, outer sterile husk or bract in the flowers of grasses (Poaceae) and sedges (Cyperaceae).

ety: Inherited from Middle English glotien /glotten, probably derived from Old French gloter /glotir /glotoiier (“to eat greedily”) [compare French engloutir (“to devour”), French glouton (“glutton”)], derived from Latin gluttiō, gluttīre (“to swallow”). Compare Russian глота́ть (glotátʹ, “to swallow”).

s.def: An excess, too much.
ex: a glut of the market
A glut of those talents which raise men to eminence.
Indeed, it was clear from the outset that anyone hoping for a repeat of last weekend's Premier League goal glut would have to look beyond St Andrew's.

s.def: That which is swallowed.
ex: And all their entrails tore, disgorging foul / Their devilish glut, […]

s.def: Something that fills up an opening.
A wooden wedge used in splitting blocks.
A piece of wood used to fill up behind cribbing or tubbing.
A bat, or small piece of brick, used to fill out a course.
An arched opening to the ashpit of a kiln.
A block used for a fulcrum.
The broad-nosed eel (Anguilla anguilla, syn. Anguilla latirostris), found in Europe, Asia, the West Indies, etc.
Five goals scored by one player in a game.
ex: Four goals scored by a single player in a match can be described as a 'haul', while five goals is unofficially a 'glut'.

ety: From glutamic acid + -ate.

s.def: Any salt or ester of glutamic acid.
The anion of glutamic acid in its role as a neurotransmitter.

ety: From glutar- + aldehyde; compare glutaric acid, glutaryl, glutarate.

s.def: The aliphatic dialdehyde pentane-1,5-dial, a toxic liquid with a pungent odor.

ety: From Middle French gluten, borrowed from Latin glūten (“glue”).

s.def: Fibrin (formerly considered as one of the "animal humours").
The major protein in cereal grains, especially wheat; responsible for the elasticity in dough and the structure in baked bread.
A gluey, sticky mass of clay, bitumen etc.
ex: Despite constant rain that turned roads to gluten, the Yankees kept moving.

s.def: Any gluey, sticky substance.
ex: [H]is nose is running in bubbly gluten over his lips onto his chin […].
The tyrant machine is the female body, grinding and milling the pulp of matter, the gluten of human flesh.

ety: From New Latin glūtæus, from Ancient Greek γλουτός (gloutós, “rump, buttock”).

s.def: Any of the several muscles of the nates, each of which arises from the pelvis and inserts into a femur.
Short for gluteus maximus, either of a pair of large muscles in the human buttocks.
ex: I'm going to kick your gluteus.

ety: From Latin glūtinōsus. By surface analysis, gluten + -ous.

s.def: Containing gluten.
Glue-like, sticky, viscid.
ex: Then comes the dinner, a glutinous spread that seems simultaneously generous and disgusting, but no one ever touches the food

s.def: Of the nature of gluten.

ety: From Middle English glotoun, from Old French gloton, gluton, from Latin gluttō, gluttōnis (“glutton”). The use for the wolverine is a semantic loan from German Vielfraß, itself a folk etymology for Old Norse *fjallfress (literally “mountain cat”). The popular belief that the wolverine is particularly voracious only developed because of this name. See the German for more.

s.def: Gluttonous; greedy; gormandizing.
ex: A glutton monastery in former ages makes a hungry ministry in our days.

s.def: One who eats voraciously, obsessively, or to excess; a gormandizer.
ex: Such a glutton would eat until his belly hurts.

s.def: One who consumes anything voraciously, obsessively, or to excess.
ex: "Gluttons in murder, wanton to destroy."
"A good few indeed, my man," replied the captain. "Yes, you may make away with a deal of money and be neither drunkard nor glutton."
Hope is a subtle glutton; / He feeds upon the fair;

s.def: The wolverine, Gulo gulo.
A giant petrel.
To glut; to satisfy (especially an appetite) by filling to capacity.
ex: Glutton'd at last, return at home to pine.

s.def: To glut; to eat voraciously.
ex: Whereon in Egypt gluttoning they fed.
Thus do I pine and surfeit day by day, / Or gluttoning on all, or all away.

ety: From Middle English glotenose, glotenouse, glotonos, glotonous, glotounius, glotynous, from Middle French glotonos; equivalent to glutton + -ous.

s.def: Given to excessive eating; prone to overeating.
ex: Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners.

s.def: Greedy.
ex: Then they could smile and fawn upon his debts, / And take down the interest into their gluttonous maws.
Look your last on your dearest ones, / Brothers and husbands, fathers, sons: / Swift they go to the ravenous guns, / The gluttonous guns of War.

ety: From Old French glutonie, from gloton + -ie, from Latin glutio, equivalent to glutton + -y.

s.def: The vice of eating to excess.

ety: Etymology tree Proto-Hellenic *dlukús Ancient Greek γλῠκῠ́ς (glŭkŭ́s)der. English glyc- Ancient Greek αἷμᾰ (haîmă)der. New Latinder. English -emia English glycemia Proto-Indo-European *-ikos Proto-Italic *-ikos Latin -icuslbor. Old French -iquebor. Middle English -ik English -ic English glycemic From glycemia + -ic.

s.def: Of, pertaining to or suffering from glycemia.
ex: The true glycemic function consists in active nutritive changes which prepare, transform and utilize the sugary materials of the blood.

ety: Introduced 1981 by David J. Jenkins et al.

s.def: A measure of the rate at which blood sugar levels rise after eating a particular type of food, on a scale where the index of glucose or ordinary table sugar is 100.

ety: Etymology tree Ancient Greek γλῠκερός (glŭkerós) Proto-Indo-European *-nós Proto-Indo-European *-iHnos Proto-Italic *-īnos Latin -īnus French -in Proto-Indo-European *-h₂ Proto-Indo-European *-eh₂ Proto-Italic *-ā Latin -am Old French -e French -e French -ine French glycérine English glycerine From glyco- + -ine, from French glycérine, from Ancient Greek γλυκερός (glukerós, “sweet”) (compare γλυκύς (glukús, “sweet”)).

s.def: Dismal and gloomy, cold and forbidding.
ex: Life was grim in many northern industrial towns.
It's been a grim start to the year.

s.def: Rigid and unrelenting.
ex: His grim determination enabled him to win.

s.def: Ghastly or sinister.
ex: A grim castle overshadowed the village.

s.def: Disgusting; gross.
ex: – Wanna see the dead rat I found in my fridge? – Mate, that is grim!

s.def: Fierce, cruel, furious.
ex: Besides what the grim wolf with privy paw / Daily devours apace, and nothing said.

s.def: To make grim; to give a stern or forbidding aspect to.
A promiscuous woman.
Anger, wrath.
A specter, ghost, haunting spirit.

ety: From grim + reaper, first attested 1847. The word grim previously had a stronger meaning ("fierce, angry, sinister") and had more of an association with ghostliness (compare Old English grima (“specter, apparition”), English grim (n.)). The association between grim and death dates back to at least the late 16th century (the line "grim death, how foul and loathsome is thine image" appears in Shakespeare's The Taming of the Shrew around 1590). The reaper element comes from the personification of…

s.def: A personification of Death as an old man, or a skeleton, carrying a scythe, taking souls to the afterlife.
ex: Her husband was dead, and Werper fancied that he could replace in the girl’s heart the position which had been vacated by the act of the grim reaper.
"Golly, I feel like the devil!" muttered Anthony dispassionately. Relaxing, he tumbled back upon his pillow. "Bring on your grim reaper!"
But that is the likely outcome if the railway waits for Treasury's grim reaper to come a-calling.

ety: From French grimace, from Middle French grimace, from Old French grimace, grimuche, from grime (“mask”) (with the pejorative suffix -ace, from Latin -āceus), from Frankish *grīma, *grīmō (“mask”), from Proto-Germanic *grīmô (“mask, helmet”). Cognate with Old English grīma (“mask, visor, helmet, spectre, apparition”). More at grime.

s.def: A contorted facial expression, often expressing contempt or pain.
ex: Her face was twisted in a grimace of disgust.
I trundle off to bed, eyes brimming, face twisted into a grateful glistening grimace, and awaken the next day wondering what all the fuss was about.

s.def: Affectation, pretence.
ex: Charlotte was equally insensible to all his fashionable grimace, and indifferent to his conversation.

s.def: To make grimaces; to distort one's face; to make faces.

ety: From grey + malkin; literally "grey-haired cat" or "grey-haired woman".

s.def: A cat, especially an elderly female.
A bad-tempered old woman; a crone.

ety: From Middle English grim (“dirt or soot covering the face”), from a specialized use of Old English grīma (“mask”), from Proto-West Germanic *grīmō, from Proto-Germanic *grīmô (“mask”). Likely influenced by dialectal Dutch grijmsel (“grit, grime”), Dutch grijm (“soot, grime”), Middle Dutch gryme (“mask”), Middle Low German greme (“dirt”), compare Danish grime (“a halter”), Danish grimet (“soiled, stripy”), Norwegian Bokmål grimete (“soiled, stripy”), Norwegian Nynorsk grimete (“soiled, stripy”).

s.def: Dirt, grease, soot, etc. that is ingrained and difficult to remove.
ex: Underneath all that soot, dirt and grime is the true beauty of the church in soft shades of sandstone.

s.def: A genre of urban music that emerged in London, England, in the early 2000s, primarily a development of UK garage, dancehall, and hip hop.
To begrime; to cake with dirt.
ex: All grimed with coaldust, they swing along the street with their dinner baskets and cans in their hands, chattering merrily.
Fog from the river rolled up the street and the windows were grimed by soot, but Cartwright had not turned on the electric light.
His skin was grimed with dust, for he had ridden hard in scorching heat, and was anxious and impatient to get on.

ety: From Middle English grinnen, from Old English grennian, from Proto-West Germanic *grannjōn, from Proto-Germanic *granjōną. Related to groan. Compare to Middle High German grennen (“to mutter, complain”) and Danish grine (“to show one's teeth, to laugh”)

s.def: A smile in which the lips are parted to reveal the teeth.
ex: When the ceremony was finished a wide grin broke across his face, and it was that grin she saw, relieved and happy all at once.
When my son appeared at the door the next day with his schoolbag on his back, the Professor broke into a wide grin and opened his arms to embrace him.

s.def: To smile, parting the lips so as to show the teeth.
ex: Why do you grin? Did I say something funny?

s.def: To express by grinning.
ex: She grinned pleasure at his embarrassment.
Grinned horrible a ghastly smile.

s.def: To show the teeth, like a snarling dog.
ex: The pangs of death do make him grin.

s.def: To grin as part of producing a particular facial expression, such as a smile or sneer.
ex: He grinned a broad smile when I told him the result.
He grinned a cruel sneer when I begged him to stop.

s.def: A snare; a gin.

der: grin like a mule eating briars

ety: Attested since at least the 1780s. The reason why Cheshire was combined with cat is disputed: see here for more information.

s.def: To smile broadly, especially in a self-satisfied way.
ex: John ended the set with a beautiful serve, an ace, and could not help grinning like a Cheshire cat.
CHESHIRE CAT. He grins like a Cheshire cat; said of any one who shows his teeth and gums in laughing.
Lo, like a Cheshire cat our court will grin.

ety: From Middle English grynden, from Old English grindan (“to grind”), from Proto-West Germanic *grindan, from Proto-Germanic *grindaną (“to crush, grind”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian gríende, griene (“to grind, mill”), West Frisian grintsje (“to crush, punish”), Dutch grinden (“to grind”, rare) and grind (“gravel, shingle”), Albanian grind (“to brawl, fight”).

s.def: To reduce to smaller pieces by crushing with lateral motion.
To remove material by rubbing with an abrasive surface.
To shape with the force of friction.
ex: grind a lens; grind an axe

s.def: To become ground, pulverized, or polished by friction.
ex: This corn grinds well.
Steel grinds to a sharp edge.

s.def: To move with much difficulty or friction; to grate.
To slide the flat portion of a skateboard or snowboard across an obstacle such as a railing.
To oppress, hold down or weaken.
To rotate the hips erotically.
ex: She said, "How'd you like to waste some time?" / And I could not resist when I saw little Nikki grind

s.def: To dance in a sexually suggestive way with both partners in very close proximity, often pressed against each other.
To rub one's body against another's in a sexual way; to frottage.
ex: She wanted to grind herself against him, wanted to moan, loud and free, wanted to take his hand and make him touch her more firmly.
He ground against her until he was muttering curses, his kiss rougher than before.
She kept grinding until they were both spent: their bliss washing over them entirely.

ety: From Middle English grinder, grindere, from Old English grindere (“one or that which grinds; grinder”), equivalent to grind + -er.

s.def: A kitchen gadget for processing coffee, herbs etc. into small or powdered pieces.
One who grinds something, such as the teeth.
ex: scissors grinder (one who sharpens scissors)
Masseter hypertrophy may become apparent in persistent grinders.

s.def: A molar.
Any tooth.
Any of various machines or devices that grind things, such as by grinding them down or grinding them up.
A sandwich made on a long, cylindrical roll.
ex: I am going to the deli to get a grinder for lunch.

s.def: The restless flycatcher (Myiagra inquieta) of Australia, which makes a noise like a scissors grinder.
A fan or performer of grindcore music.
A biohacker who uses cybernetic implants or biochemicals to enhance or change their own body.
A student who studies hard; a swot.

ety: From grind + -ery.

s.def: The materials used by leatherworkers.
A mill where something is ground.

ety: From Middle English grind-ston, grindistan, (also as grindel-ston), equivalent to grind + stone. Cognate with Scots grindstane.

s.def: An abrasive wheel for sharpening, polishing, or grinding.
Synonym of starry flounder.

ety: Borrowed from Spanish gringo, from griego (“Greek”), used for anyone who spoke an unintelligible language. Doublet of Greek.

s.def: A white person from an English-speaking country, particularly the United States.
ex: Truly it is as Don José tells me; these gringos have come but to make trouble where all was peace.

ety: Verb from Middle English grippen, from Old English grippan, from a Proto-Germanic *gripjaną (compare Old High German gripfen); compare the related Old English grīpan, whence English gripe. See also grope, and the related Proto-Germanic *grīpaną. Noun from Middle English grippe, gripe, an amalgam of Old English gripe (“grasp, hold”) (cognate with German Griff) and Old English gripa (“handful”) (cognate with Swedish grepp).

s.def: To take hold (of), particularly with the hand.
ex: That suitcase is heavy, so grip the handle firmly.
Unfortunately the glue didn't grip, and the whole thing came apart.
After a few slips, the tires gripped the pavement.

s.def: To figuratively take hold of or grasp.
ex: We need to grip this problem, not shut our eyes and hope it goes away.

s.def: Of an emotion or situation: to have a strong effect upon.
ex: As the water level began to rise, I was gripped by panic.
[…] I lost something of the stifling fear that had gripped me, and could listen with more ease to what was going forward.

s.def: To firmly hold the attention of.
ex: The movie gripped me from beginning to end.

s.def: A hold or way of holding, particularly with the hand.
ex: It's good to have a firm grip when shaking hands.
The ball will move differently depending on the grip used when throwing it.

s.def: Ability to resist slippage when pressed in contact with another object or surface.
ex: These tyres are worn out and don't have much grip.

s.def: A place to grip; a handle; the portion of a handle that the hand occupies.
ex: Near-synonym: handgrip
There are several good grips on the northern face of this rock.
The grip of a sword is part of its hilt.

s.def: A device, or a portion of one, that grasps or holds fast to something.
ex: The unthreaded portion of the bolt's shank is called the grip.

s.def: Control, power, or mastery over someone or something; a tenacious grasp; a holding fast.
ex: We need to get a grip on these spiralling costs.
in the grip of a blackmailer
to strengthen one's grip on a company

s.def: Mental grasp.
ex: He's losing his grip – he's practically senile.
For God's sake man, stop panicking and get a grip of yourself!

ety: From Middle English gripen, from Old English grīpan, from Proto-Germanic *grīpaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreyb- (“to grab, grasp”). Cognate with West Frisian gripe, Low German griepen, Dutch grijpen, German greifen, Danish gribe, Norwegian Bokmål gripe, Norwegian Nynorsk and Swedish gripa, Icelandic grípa. See also grip, grope.

s.def: To complain; to whine.
To annoy or bother.
ex: What's griping you?

s.def: To tend to come up into the wind, as a ship which, when sailing close-hauled, requires constant labour at the helm.
To pinch; to distress. Specifically, to cause pinching and spasmodic pain to the bowels of, as by the effects of certain purgative or indigestible substances.
ex: How inly sorrow gripes his soul.

s.def: To suffer griping pains.
ex: the griping of an hungry belly

s.def: To make a grab (to, towards, at or upon something).
To seize or grasp.
ex: Unclutch his griping hand.

s.def: A complaint, often a petty or trivial one.
A wire rope, often used on davits and other life raft launching systems.
Grasp; clutch; grip.
ex: A barren sceptre in my gripe.
The young peasant […] disengaged himself from Manfred's gripe […].

ety: Borrowed from French grippe, from gripper (“to seize, snatch”), from Frankish *grīpan, from Proto-Germanic *grīpaną, from Proto-Indo-European *gʰreyb- (“to grab, to grasp”). Borrowed from French into many languages of the world. More at gripe.

s.def: Influenza, the flu.
ex: These other germs are the cause of colds and coughs and grippes.
[T]hat day was the only holiday I had all the time I was in camp - except when I had the ‘grippe’ and nearly pegged out.

ety: Etymology tree English grip Proto-Indo-European *-yósder. Proto-Italic *-āzios Latin -āriusnom. Latin -āriusbor. Proto-Germanic *-ārijaz Proto-West Germanic *-ārī Old English -ere Middle English -ere English -er English gripper From grip + -er.

s.def: A ticket collector.
A visual component on a window etc. enabling it to be resized and/or moved.
A person who or thing which grips something.
A cover on a handle that makes it easier to grip.
A rubber or other material attached to a curling shoe to improve traction on the ice.
A foot.
ex: Put those grippers away!

ety: Unadapted borrowing from French grisaille.

s.def: In painting, a method of working which employs only varying values of gray to create form. Often a preliminary step in a fully colored painting.
A stained-glass window in this style.

ety: From Medieval Latin grīseus, from Proto-West Germanic *grīs (“grey”) (for which compare French gris and German greis) and -eus.

s.def: Having a gray, mottled appearance

ety: Borrowed from French grisette, from gris (“grey”) + -ette, named after the color of the fabric associated with low value or bad quality.

s.def: A (chiefly French) girl or young married woman of the lower class; especially, a young working-class woman of perceived easy morals.
ex: ‘What a fuss is here, indeed, about a little grisette: why, one would think Beresford had carried off an heiress.’
The anticipations of the shopkeeper were realized, and his rooms soon became notorious through the charms of the sprightly grisette.
[…]Paris from afar sounded its fanfare of masked balls with the laugh of grisettes.

s.def: The grisette amanita (Amanita vaginata), an edible mushroom in the amanita family.
A variety of low-alcohol beer that is light in body, with a noticeable tartness similar to other farmhouse ales.
ex: Oral accounts of those who remember the old grisettes say they were low-alcohol, light-bodied, saison-like golden ales of no great distinction.
She talked animatedly, with her hands, and her excitement about something as boring as the differences between a saison and a grisette was contagious.

ety: From Middle English grisely, grysly, grissliȝ, griselich, grislich, from Old English grisliċ (“grisly, horrible; dreadful, horrid”), from grīsan (“to shudder with horror; to tremble, to be terrified; to make tremble, to terrify; to agrise, grise”) (unattested but implied in āgrīsan) + -lic (suffix forming adjectives meaning ‘characteristic of, pertaining to’). The word may also be an aphetic form of Old English ongrislic, agrisenliċ, the past participle of agrīsan (“to agrise”). Compare Danish…

s.def: Horrifyingly repellent; gruesome, terrifying.
ex: The photographs of the killings depict a grisly scene.
Then clad in cloake of mistie fogges the darke night vp did come, / And with grim grislie looke did seeme to bid me get me home; […]
Ireland’s capital is no longer in lockdown but the grisly sport continues.

s.def: Obsolete form of grizzly.
ex: old squirrels that turn grisly
The animals found in this province are, deer, elk, buffalo, cabrie, the grisly black bear, and wild horses.

s.def: Misspelling of gristly.
Obsolete form of grizzly (“type of bear”).
In a horrible or terrible manner; in a terrifying way.

ety: From Middle English grist, gryst, from Old English grist, gyrst (“the action of grinding, corn for grinding, gnashing”), of obscure origin: possibly from a pre-Germanic substrate language, or from a derivative of Proto-Germanic *gredaną (“to crunch”), possibly from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer- (“to rub, grind”). Cognate with Old Saxon gristgrimmo (“gnashing of the teeth”), German Griesgram (“a grumbler, a grouch, peevishness, misery”), Old English gristel (“gristle”).

s.def: Grain that is to be ground in a mill.
A group of bees.
ex: Swarming like a grist of bees...
A grist of bees is somehow leaking through the insufficient squares of the bug screen

s.def: Supply; provision.
ex: Matter, as wise logicians say, / Cannot without a form subsist; / And form, say I, as well as they, / Must fail if matter brings no grist.

s.def: A given size of rope, common grist being a rope three inches in circumference, with twenty yarns in each of the three strands.
Ellipsis of grist for the mill.
To grind in a mill.
ex: […] and another mill is erecting on the same stream near Sparrow Lake, to which a run of stones for gristing will be added.
[…] it cleaned out two hundred and ten bushels called screenings; the balance was sold, gristed and used for seed.

ety: With early modern vowel shortening, from Middle English grete, griet, from Old English grēot, from Proto-West Germanic *greut, from Proto-Germanic *greutą. Compare grist.

s.def: A collection of hard small materials, such as dirt, ground stone, debris from sandblasting or other such grinding, or swarf from metalworking.
ex: The flower beds were white with grit from sand blasting the flagstone walkways.

s.def: Small, hard, inedible particles in food.
ex: These cookies seem to have grit from nutshells in them.

s.def: A measure of the size of abrasive grains, such as those on sandpaper, and thus their relative coarseness or fineness; the smaller the number, the coarser the abrasive: thus, 60 is rough, 600 is fine, and 3000 is ultrafine.
ex: I need a sheet of 100 grit sandpaper.

s.def: A hard, coarse-grained siliceous sandstone; gritstone. Also, a finer sharp-grained sandstone, e.g., grindstone grit.
Strength of mind; courage or fearlessness; fortitude.
ex: That kid with the cast on his arm has the grit to play dodgeball.
They came to a rising ground , not sharp , but long ; and here youth and grit and sober living told more than ever.
If you are overcome by a man of grit, he insolently makes you conscious of your own weakness

s.def: To clench (one's teeth), particularly in reaction to pain or anger.
ex: We had no choice but to grit our teeth and get on with it.
He has a sleeping disorder and grits his teeth.
My teeth gritted as I heard the news.

s.def: To cover with grit.
To give forth a grating sound, like sand under the feet; to grate; to grind.
ex: The sanded floor that grits beneath the tread

s.def: Husked but unground oats.
Coarsely ground corn or hominy used as porridge.
ex: grits and eggs
ham and grits

ety: See grit (Etymology 2, “hulled oats”).

s.def: plural of grit ('hulled oats'); groats.
Coarsely ground hominy which is boiled and eaten, primarily in the Southern United States.
plural of grit
third-person singular simple present indicative of grit

ety: Etymology tree English grit Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Germanic *-gaz Proto-West Germanic *-g Old English -iġ Middle English -y English -y English gritty From grit + -y.

s.def: Containing sand or grit; consisting of grit; caused by grit; full of hard particles.
Spirited; resolute; unyielding.
ex: That goth woman is very gritty.
The runt was the grittiest pup of all; for days he writhed out of one convulsion into the next—calmed from one only to go through it all over again.

s.def: Intense and starkly realistic; depicting harsh reality, especially violence.

ety: From Middle English grisel, gryselle, from Old French grisel, from gris (“grey”), from Frankish *grīs, from Proto-Germanic *grīsaz.

s.def: A dark grey colour.
Grey hair.
A grey wig.
Of a grey colour.
To make or become grey, as with age.
ex: R. F. Burton hardship of the way such as would grizzle little children
Pall Mall Magazine I found myself on the Nubian desert shaking hands with a grizzling man whom men addressed as Collins Bey.

s.def: To cry continuously but not very loudly (said especially of young children).
To whinge or whine.
ex: R. J. Tizard — What are you grizzling about now?
The pin-thin girl is grizzling, whining that she has sand in her eyes.

s.def: To fuss or cry.
ex: New mothers frequently complain that their partner won't get up to change a wet nappy or comfort a grizzling baby.

ety: Etymology tree English grizzle Proto-Indo-European *-kos Proto-Germanic *-gaz Proto-West Germanic *-g Old English -iġ Middle English -y English -y English grizzly From grizzle + -y.

s.def: Grey-haired, greyish.
Misspelling of grisly.
ex: This after Taliban militants led a grizzly campaign of attacks, including beheadings, kidnappings and the destruction of dozens of girls' schools.

s.def: A grizzly bear.
ex: Shotgun blast kills charging grizzly!

s.def: A grating used to sieve stones by size, so as to keep stones out of the sluices (in hydraulic mining) or to control stone size in the feed to the ore crusher.
Crying or whingeing in a bad-tempered or irritable way.
ex: a grizzly baby

ety: From Middle English gronen, granen, from Old English grānian (“to groan; lament; murmur”), from Proto-West Germanic *grainōn, from Proto-Germanic *grainōną (“to howl; weep”), from Proto-Germanic *grīnaną (“to whine; howl; whimper”). Cognate with Scots grain (“to cry, scream”), Dutch grijnen, grienen (“to cry; sob; blubber”), German Low German grienen (“to whimper; mewl”), German greinen (“to whine; whimper”), Swedish grina (“to howl; weep; laugh”). The noun is from Middle English gron, grone, f…

s.def: A low, mournful sound uttered in pain or grief.
ex: let out a groan

s.def: A low, guttural sound uttered in frustration, disapproval, or ecstasy.
A low creaking sound from applied pressure or weight.
To make a groan.
ex: We groaned at his awful jokes.
The wooden table groaned under the weight of the banquet.

s.def: To seemingly creak under the strain of being heavily laden.
ex: That night the table in the outer dining room was just groaning with good things.
Bookshelves groan under the bloated weight of tomes detailing Great Straight Marriages.

s.def: To strive after earnestly, as if with groans.
ex: Nothing but holy, pure, and clear, / Or that which groaneth to be so.

ety: From Middle English gronynge (“groaning”), from Old English grānung; equivalent to groan + -ing. Conflated with Middle English gronende, present participle of gronen, from Old English grāniende, present participle of grānian (“to groan”). Analyzable as groan + -ing.

s.def: That groans.
Heavily laden, as if to creak under the strain.
ex: We sat down to a groaning table and feasted all evening.

s.def: A low sound associated with extended suffering, sorrow, and toil.
ex: From the nearby rail yards came clangings, groanings, chuggings.

s.def: Ellipsis of groaning time (“childbirth, labour”).

ety: From Middle English grot, from Old English grot, from Proto-West Germanic *grot, from Proto-Germanic *grutą, related to *greutą. More at grit, grout.

s.def: Hulled grain, chiefly hulled oats.
Any of various old coins of England and Scotland.
ex: The needy groom, that never finger'd groat, Would make a miracle of thus much coin …

s.def: A proverbial small sum; a whit or jot.
plural of groat

ety: From Old French grossier (“wholesaler”). Compare gross.

s.def: A person who retails groceries (foodstuffs and household items) from a grocery.
ex: “Cadiz isn't going to become the garbage dump capital of the world,” said Patrick Erbacher, a grocer who is vice president of the Cadiz Jaycees.

s.def: A retail store that sells groceries, a grocery store.
To sell groceries; to act as a grocer.

ety: From Middle English grocerye, equivalent to grocer + -y. Compare gross. Doublet of groceria.

s.def: Retail foodstuffs and other household supplies.
A shop or store that sells groceries; a grocery store.
ex: 1854: Henry David Thoreau, Walden I observed that the vitals of the village were the grocery, the bar-room, the post-office, and the bank...

s.def: To go grocery shopping.
ex: We shopped and groceried on a cash basis, determined on that from the start.
The thought of grocerying so casually at Seessel's evokes a giggle from Shirley
I was dependent upon others for grocerying and getting to doctor appointments.

s.def: To furnish with groceries.
ex: Fifty-eight years of grocerying hotels, restaurants and institutions that feed many people
What freedom to be iced, fueled, and groceried for two weeks and running toward a reef you truly love

s.def: A store where groceries can be purchased, especially a supermarket.

ety: An allusion to Admiral Edward Vernon (nicknamed “Old Grog” after the grogram coat he habitually wore), who in 1740 ordered his sailors' rum to be watered down. Alternatively, from Old Catalan grog or groch, modern groc, meaning "yellow" (ultimately from Latin crocum (“saffron”); after the name of the resulting color of the watered down rum sold all over the Mediterranean. The ration of rum tot could also come from Catalan tot meaning "full", "whole".

s.def: An alcoholic beverage made with rum and water, especially that once issued to sailors of the Royal Navy.
Any alcoholic beverage.
A glass or serving of an alcoholic beverage.
A type of pre-fired clay that has been ground and screened to a specific particle size.
To grind and screen (clay) to a specific particle size.
To drink alcohol.

ety: From grog + -y.

s.def: Slowed or weakened, as by drink, sleepiness, etc.
ex: The medicine made him groggy and irritable.

s.def: Of a horse: bearing wholly on its heels when trotting.

ety: Borrowed from French gros-grain (“coarse grain, a strong fabric”), from gros (“coarse”) + grain (“grain”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *ǵerh₂- (“to grow old, mature”)). The word is a doublet of grosgrain which was borrowed later.

s.def: A strong, rough fabric made up of a mixture of silk, and mohair or wool.
A garment made from this fabric.

The area adjoining this fold or depression.
ex: He pulled a muscle in his groin.

s.def: The projecting solid angle formed by the meeting of two vaults
The surface formed by two such vaults.
The genitals.
ex: He got kicked in the groin and was writhing in pain.

s.def: To deliver a blow to the genitals of.
ex: In the scrum he somehow got groined.

To hollow out; to excavate.
ex: Down some profound dull tunnel, long since scooped / Through granites which titanic wars had groined.

ex: Beares, that groynd continually

s.def: US standard spelling of groyne.

ety: Coined ex nihilo by American author and engineer Robert A. Heinlein in 1961 in his novel Stranger in a Strange Land. Heinlein invented the word for his fictitious Martian language. It is described as meaning "to drink" and, figuratively, "to drink in all available aspects of reality", "to become one with the observed". William Tenn asked Heinlein if it could have been inspired by the term griggo, which featured in Tenn's "Venus and the Seven Sexes" (1949); Heinlein "looked startled, then though…

ex: It was at this town of Badajoz, the capital of Estremadura, that I first fell in with those singular people, the Zincali, Gitanos, or Spanish gypsies.

s.def: Alternative form of Gypsy: of or belonging to the Rom, Dom or Lom people.
Of or having the qualities of an itinerant person or group with qualities traditionally ascribed to Romani people; making a living from dishonest practices or theft etc.
To roam around the country like a gypsy.
ex: The rest of the day is spent out of doors "Gypsying", and families greatly enjoy themselves on these occasions.

s.def: a member of the Romani people or another nomadic group
A member of the Romani people, or one of the sub-groups (Roma, Sinti, Romanichal, etc).
A member of other nomadic peoples, not only of the Romani people; a traveller. Alternative spelling of gypsy.

ety: Back-formation from gyration, on the basis of -ate (verb-forming suffix), from gyre (“to spin around; to gyrate, to whirl; (rare) to make (something) spin or whirl around; to spin, to whirl”) + -ation (suffix indicating actions or processes), further from Late Middle English giren (“to turn (something) away; to cause (something) to revolve or rotate; to travel in a circle”), from Old French girer (“to turn”), from Latin gȳrō (“to turn in a circle, rotate; to circle or revolve around”), from gȳr…

s.def: To revolve round a central point; to move spirally about an axis, as a tornado.
ex: The stripper gyrated sexily around a pole.
Many companies built up pretariff inventories, and gyrating tariff rates make it tricky for retailers to set prices.

s.def: Having coils or convolutions.

ety: Borrowed from Latin gȳrus (“circle; circular motion”), from Ancient Greek γῦρος (gûros, “circle; ring”), from Proto-Indo-European *gew- (“to bend; to curve”). The English word is a doublet of gyro and gyrus.

s.def: A swirling vortex.
A circular or spiral motion; also, a circle described by a moving body; a revolution, a turn.
Synonym of gyrus (“a fold or ridge on the cerebral cortex of the brain”).
An ocean current caused by wind which moves in a circular manner, especially one that is large-scale and observed in a major ocean.
ex: Most ships that tried to cross the Pacific in the past would get stuck in the gyres and never make it out.

s.def: To spin around; to gyrate, to whirl.
ex: Jabberwocky. / 'Twas brillig, and the slithy toves / Did gyre and gimble in the wa[b]e; / All mimsy were the borogoves, / And the mome raths outgrabe.

s.def: To make (something) spin or whirl around; to spin, to whirl.

ety: From Old French gerfaucon (modern French gerfaut), with the first element probably from Old High German gīr (“vulture”) (whence the German Geier).

s.def: Falco rusticolus, a large bird of prey that breeds on Arctic coasts and islands of North America, Europe and Asia.
Any large falcon, especially as used to fly at herons.

s.def: A device for stabilizing using a gyroscope.
